section_title: How does the church respond when Herod attacks its members?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 1 About that time, King Herod reached out to harm some who belonged to the church. 2 He had James, the brother of John, put to death with the sword. 3 And seeing that this pleased the Jews, Herod proceeded to seize Peter during the Feast of Unleavened Bread. 4 He arrested him and put him in prison, handing him over to be guarded by four squads of four soldiers each. Herod intended to bring him out to the people after the Passover. 5 So Peter was kept in prison, but the church was fervently praying to God for him.

context_lines: After the report of growth and relief for Judea, Luke describes renewed persecution. Herod has James, the brother of John, killed with the sword. This is one of the sons of Zebedee who followed Jesus, not the James Peter will mention later in the chapter.

Herod sees that this pleases the Jews and arrests Peter as well. The arrest takes place during the Feast of Unleavened Bread. Peter is guarded by four squads of four soldiers each, and Herod plans to bring him before the people after Passover.

The church’s response is fervent prayer to God for Peter. Luke sets that prayer beside the king’s confinement of him. James has died, Peter remains in danger, and the believers are appealing to God in circumstances they cannot control.
common_interpretation_lines: Christians commonly read the church’s prayer as active concern for a fellow believer under persecution. [Calvin on verse 5](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/acts/12.htm) emphasizes sharing the burden of those suffering for the gospel rather than abandoning them.
god_plan_lines: In [Mark 10:35–40](https://biblehub.com/bsb/mark/10.htm), James and John ask for places of honor, and Jesus tells them they will share His cup of suffering. James’s death belongs within that costly pattern of following Jesus, rather than proving that his discipleship has failed.

Luke does not explain James’s death by comparing the quality of his faith with Peter’s. The wider story of witness includes both lives given in service and dramatic deliverances; this chapter does not provide a formula for predicting which outcome any believer will receive.
